tellings.difference: Puthoff tells it firsthand and adds that it ran 20 years on $20 million, growing out of remote viewing of secret facilities and project titles locked in safes, but he doesn't mention Ed May or doubts about how well it worked.

as_told.title: Russell Targ and Hal Puthoff founded the CIA psychic spy program Stargate

plain: From 1972 to 1995, the US government is said to have paid people to spy with their minds in a programme called Stargate. It used "remote viewing", the attempt to describe distant or hidden places by mental focus alone. Jesse Michels returns to it often and says it was backed first by the CIA and later by the Defense Intelligence Agency, the military's spy service. He says its targets included Russian nuclear bases and American hostages, and that its files were released in 2017 under FOIA, a US law that lets anyone request government records. The physicist Hal Puthoff, who helped found it with Russell Targ, tells it from the inside: it began with viewing secret facilities and project names locked in safes and grew into "a 20-year 20 million dollar program". Joe McMoneagle, who took part as a viewer, says it had the support of five presidents and senators such as John Glenn, and that it ended because of stigma, not because it failed. Michels notes that many said afterward it was not very effective, and that the official reason for closing it was that it offered "only offense" and no defence. Others back it up in their own ways: the whistleblower David Grusch passes on what Puthoff told him about viewers' reports being confirmed by normal intelligence, the former Pentagon official Luis Elizondo calls Puthoff the programme's "Godfather", and a former official named Matthew Brown talks about the trouble of putting psychics on the payroll. If it worked as they say, governments really did use the mind as a spying tool.
